title: Differences between Black and white bands and who listened to whom
summary: Goodwin says white and Black bands sounded distinct, white musicians came to hear Black bands, and jazz grew from the blues.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, right. I just wanted to get that in. Here is an interesting question prepared by Mr. Taylor at the Performing Arts. As you traveled, Baby and Crook, what regional style differences did you notice; the style of music by region? What style differences existed between black and white musicians as you traveled? I would say here in Kansas City and as you left Kansas City, the differences between the black and the white musicians?
Now assuming perhaps that the white musicians played

differently from the black, was that difference greater than the regional differences? For example, was the music more different in Chicago than Kansas City, the way it was played, and the differences in the way white and black musicians played? I hope I've made that question clear.
Can I answer this?
Crook Goodwin.

There was a difference. I can remember back in the '30s, early '30s and late '30s, that you would listen to a white band and you could tell this was a white band. You listened to a black band, you could tell this was a black band. There was a distinct difference; now however, the black bands tend to play a little louder than the white bands. I mean the old band and -- but the white bands seemed to me wanted to play what the black bands were playing.

I would notice this because I noticed being here in Kansas City, which was a center for most bands to come through on the circuit or two or three circuits here, they'd come and play the big theaters here. Well, they would all -- all the white musicians mostly would come out where the black musicians were and I think this --
Well, that's always interesting and I often wondered and I'm going to ask you, do black musicians ever go where the white musicians were to hear anything they
were doing; not only here in Kansas City but other cities?
Very seldom, very seldom.
I suppose one reason was they weren't welcome in a white room?

That's right, see, but I have noticed since I first started in music that the bulk of the white musicians would come out to where -- if there was a good black band, they would come out and I noticed oh back in those days well, you know, when you'd wear these stiff cuffs --
Detachable cuffs.
-- the arrangers would come out and they would hear things that the black musicians were playing and they would write down on their cuff, you know, the different things.
When I was a boy growing up in Boston we always felt that jazz, to be really good, had to be played by black musicians, to be really good.
Well, this was the case back in the '30s --
and 40s.
-- and the early '40s but --

Of course I realize now that there are a tremendous number of white musicians playing terrific jazz music and there always has been but there was always a feeling in those days that if it was jazz it had to be by black
musicians.

Well it more or less started from the black musicians because it's a thing between the blues and oh -- and just -- well you can -- it's just a combination of music, you know; what you might call pop music, blues and I think that --
Shall we say that there was a soul factor added to it?
Right. I think that this was because the black man always had some worries, you know.
He lived the blues?
He lived the blues.
I always felt to play the blues you had to live them.
That's right.
